summary: Gives the IAB's evaluation of the present and near-term effects of CIDR on organizations using classful routing technology. It is informational and now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains the effect of CIDR on organizations using older classful routing. Sites without CIDR-capable routing may have to use a default route, which can produce less direct paths.

questions: how does cidr affect classful routing
what did the iab say about cidr
why can a default route be suboptimal
subtitle: Describes how CIDR affects organizations that still use classful routing protocols.

tldr.problem: CIDR-based address allocation and route aggregation require routing support that older classful protocols do not provide.
tldr.mechanism: The memo identifies which routing protocols support variable-length subnet masks and CIDR and explains that other sites may need to rely on a default route.
tldr.outcome: Organizations seeking to avoid potentially suboptimal default routing need CIDR-capable routing. Unit metadata classifies this RFC as Historic.

today: RFC 1817 is classified as Historic in the unit metadata. It describes CIDR's implications for organizations that use classful routing.

sections.title: What CIDR Changes
sections.content:
CIDR uses variable-length subnet masks and removes the old classes of network numbers A, B, and C. The memo identifies OSPF, RIP II, Integrated IS-IS, E-IGRP, and BGP-4 as protocols that support CIDR in the roles described.

It identifies RIP, BGP-3, EGP, and IGRP as protocols that do not support CIDR.
sections.plainLanguage: CIDR allows address blocks to be described without the old fixed network classes. Routers need protocols that can carry this classless routing information.

sections.title: Sites Using Classful Routing
sections.content:
A site that relies only on a default route for external connectivity may not need CIDR support in its internal routing protocol. Other sites that lack variable-length subnet mask and CIDR support must rely on a default route.

The memo warns that this can lead to different degrees of suboptimal routing. An organization that wants to avoid this effect needs to move to CIDR-capable routing protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: A site without CIDR-capable routing may send external traffic through a default route. The resulting path may be less direct than one chosen with more specific route information.

sections.title: Address Allocation and Providers
sections.content:
The memo anticipates that Internet registries will allocate blocks of variable size from former Class A address space based on the needs of sites. Sites using these blocks will need CIDR-capable routing.

It says providers are expected to support CIDR-capable routing protocols, while sites not using the new addresses could continue to rely on default routes.
sections.plainLanguage: Variable-size address allocations require routing protocols that understand CIDR. Providers are expected to support those protocols so the routes can be carried through the Internet.
